props.title: Move Over, Darling

sections.content: Move Over, Darling stands as a quintessential 1960s romantic comedy, starring Doris Day and James Garner in a delightful remake of My Favorite Wife (1940). The film tackles the amusing premise of a wife returning after being stranded on a desert island for five years, only to find her husband has just remarried. This plot device of the "returning spouse" became a popular post-war narrative, also seen in Too Many Husbands (1940) and Something's Got to Give (1962) - the infamously unfinished Marilyn Monroe version of the same story.

sections.content: The film showcases Doris Day at the height of her comedic powers, following her massive successes with Pillow Talk (1959) and That Touch of Mink (1962). Day's character Ellen Wagstaff Arden embodies the evolving role of women in 1960s cinema - she's resourceful, determined, and far from the damsel in distress, despite her castaway predicament. James Garner stepped into the role originally intended for Dean Martin, bringing his characteristic charm that he'd later perfect in The Thrill of It All (1963), another collaboration with Day.

The screwball elements of Move Over, Darling follow a rich tradition of marriage-themed comedies like The Awful Truth (1937) and The Philadelphia Story (1940). Director Michael Gordon, who had previously directed Day in Pillow Talk (1959), maintains the perfect balance of farce and romantic tension, while updating the material for 1960s sensibilities. The film's success helped cement the "comedy of remarriage" as a distinct subgenre. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Romantic Comedy

sections.content: Move Over, Darling represents a crucial transition point between the screwball comedies of the 1930s-40s and the more modern romantic comedies that would follow. The film maintains the rapid-fire dialogue and physical comedy of classics like His Girl Friday (1940) while introducing more contemporary themes about marriage and gender roles that would later influence films like Send Me No Flowers (1964) and even modern variations like Overboard (1987).
